summary: This standards-track memo defines a location object format, extending the Presence Information Data Format (PIDF), for carrying geographical information. It inherits privacy-sensitive properties of PIDF.

plainLanguage.summary: PIDF-LO packages a location with rules about how the recipient may handle it. The format can carry geographic coordinates or a civic address, and the document can be encrypted and signed.

questions: what is the geopriv location object
how does geopriv protect location privacy
how does pidf-lo protect location information
subtitle: A PIDF extension that carries geographic location together with rules for sharing and retaining it.

tldr.problem: A location format needs to carry the location together with the owner's handling preferences and protection for the whole document.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC extends PIDF with a geopriv element containing location information and usage rules, and specifies S/MIME protection for the document.
tldr.outcome: The format can carry GML or civic location information and rules about onward sharing and retention. RFC 4119 has been updated by RFC 5139, RFC 5491, and RFC 7459.

today: RFC 4119 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 5139, RFC 5491, and RFC 7459. Consult those updates for later changes to the format.

sections.title: A Location Object with Privacy Rules
sections.content:
Location information can describe where a person, event, or device was, is, or will be. Sharing it can be useful, but weak security or missing user preferences can disclose it in unwanted ways.

RFC 4119 extends the XML-based Presence Information Data Format (PIDF) so a presence document can contain location information and usage rules. It wraps existing location formats rather than defining a new way to describe geography. The format can be carried by protocols that support XML or MIME types.
sections.plainLanguage: This format puts location information and its handling rules in one presence document. It reuses existing ways to describe a place instead of defining a new geography format.

sections.title: The PIDF Document Around the Location
sections.content:
A PIDF document's entity attribute identifies the person, place, or thing the presence information describes. The URI can use the pres scheme, which can provide an unlinkable pseudonym.

The document can include an optional contact URI and timestamp. Its required status element can contain the geopriv extension. A tuple groups presence information under an identifier so changes can be tracked across updates.
sections.plainLanguage: The document identifies whose location it describes, possibly with a pseudonymous URI. Optional contact and time information can accompany the location.

sections.title: Location Information and Optional Details
sections.content:
The geopriv element has two required parts: location-info and usage-rules. The location element can contain one or more location formats, identified by their XML schemas.

Implementations that support geopriv must support the GML 3.0 feature.xsd schema. The RFC also defines a civic location format that implementations may support, with fields for country, region, city, street, house number, and other address details.

Optional method information says how the location was determined. Optional provided-by information names a provider, but can reveal extra detail about a location and is not intended for most entities.
sections.plainLanguage: The required location field can hold geographic or civic data. Optional fields can say how the location was found and who supplied it.

sections.title: Rules for Sharing and Retaining Location
sections.content:
Each geopriv element must contain usage rules, even when the rule fields use their defaults. The rules can limit onward sharing, set a time after which the recipient must discard the object, point to a fuller ruleset, and include a human-readable note.

The default for retransmission-allowed is no. The default retention period is twenty-four hours from the PIDF timestamp, or from receipt when there is no timestamp. A recipient must immediately discard an object whose retention time has already passed.

A ruleset reference should use HTTPS, and the server hosting rules must authenticate access. A CID URI can instead point to a MIME body carried with the location object.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules can say not to share the location and when to discard it. If no sharing preference is given, the recipient must assume that sharing is not allowed.

sections.title: Protecting the Whole Location Object
sections.content:
The RFC applies security to the PIDF document as a whole rather than protecting individual elements. Partial protection could reveal private information through the unprotected parts.

Implementations that support the location extensions must support S/MIME and the CMS EnvelopedData and SignedData content types for encryption and signatures. They must implement AES for S/MIME and must support password-based CMS encryption.

The RFC's security scope is the location object itself. Authentication and other security needs of the protocol carrying the object are left to that protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The document is protected as a whole so that an unprotected part cannot reveal location details. The protocol that carries it must handle its own security needs.

sections.title: Carrying the Object and Registered Terms
sections.content:
PIDF is XML and can be carried by protocols that carry XML. Its registered MIME type is application/pidf+xml, so it can also be carried as a MIME body.

The RFC creates an IANA registry for method tokens and initially registers GPS, assisted GPS, Manual, DHCP, Triangulation, Cell, and 802.11. It also registers XML namespaces for provider information and the geopriv extension.
sections.plainLanguage: Applications can carry the document wherever XML or MIME bodies are supported. A registered list gives common names for how a location was obtained.
